problem_data.story:
The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting, sinking toward the horizon beyond the western boundary of our territory. I turned to face it, squinting against the orange light. Below, stretching across the valley floor, the great agricultural domes caught the last rays of daylight. Their curved surfaces gleamed bronze and gold where the light struck them directly, but already shadows were creeping across the nearest domes from the elevated terrain to the west. The shadow line advanced slowly as I watched, swallowing dome after dome in premature twilight.

It was an old grievance among the farmers who worked these valley domes—losing nearly an hour of growing light each evening. The western ridge rose sharply from the valley floor, its silhouette dark against the setting sun. I could see the administrative buildings and Memorial Gardens perched along the ridge's edge, their elevated position ensuring they caught sunlight long after the valley below had fallen into shadow. The ridge belonged to our district, of course—Westfield's terrain encompassed both the fertile valley and the highlands that bordered it to the west.

Northfield District lay to the north and east, on lower ground that caught morning light earlier than we did. Their farmers complained about the reverse problem—our eastern hills blocked their dawn sun. Such were the compromises the Founders had made when they divided the territory.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—" she paused, choosing her words carefully, "—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir," Diana confirmed. "The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

"This is a matter for the High Command," I said carefully. In moments of crisis, one must speak with precision. "Summon the War Council immediately."

The two young officers ran ahead while I made my way down to Command Center at a more measured pace. A man my age doesn't rush, even in emergencies. Besides, I needed time to think.

The genetic vault had been established after the Climate Wars, when radiation and environmental toxins had damaged much of humanity's genetic diversity. The Founders had created machines to preserve and, when necessary, generate new genetic combinations to prevent inbreeding and genetic disease. For three hundred years, the system had worked flawlessly, producing healthy children through the Gestation Chambers while maintaining genetic diversity.

And now it was gone.

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled, waiting for me to call them to order. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain. They had earned the right to see this through.

The meeting proceeded as these things do. Many officers felt compelled to make speeches. Prayers were offered to the memory of the Founders. Technical teams were dispatched to assess the damage. Finally, as the emergency lighting began to activate with the onset of night, the Chief Medical Officer was given the floor.

Dr. Theodore Willis was the oldest among us, his white hair and weathered face testament to a lifetime of service. He smoothed his beard—a habit when nervous—and addressed the Council.

"I will not burden you with technical details that only the Founders truly understood," he began. "The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. This has been our system since the Founder Wars."

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the room.

"But now," he continued, his voice faltering, "we face an unprecedented situation. A true emergency. The vault has failed completely. All preserved genetic material has been destroyed. The Gestation Chambers cannot function without it. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. Officers shouted, some called for Willis's resignation, others demanded impossible solutions. I restored order with difficulty, grateful that the War Council was composed entirely of senior officers. Men and women in their sixties and seventies can only sustain outrage for so long.

When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"As I explained," Willis replied, "given even a small sample, the machines can generate more. But without that initial material, they are useless."

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied in his characteristically infuriating manner. "Must there not, three centuries ago, have been a source of genetic material—a source now forgotten? And might it not still be available to us, if we could remember? I'm reminded of the historical records of the pre-Founder era—"

"Your mind is wandering, General," I interrupted. "What do the ancient records have to do with our current crisis?"

The Council members were looking at me expectantly. I sighed and explained. "General Stewart refers to records from before the Founder Wars, describing a time when humans reproduced without technological assistance. But those records are fragmentary, often contradictory, and generally considered unreliable folklore."

Stewart's voice cut through the murmurs. "Not folklore, Colonel. Historical fact. The archaeological evidence is clear. The data science analysis of pre-Founder populations proves it conclusively. Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana, standing at attention by the door, hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"If this is true," I said slowly, "how did this biological reproduction function?"

"That," Stewart replied, "is precisely what I propose to discover. I request permission to access the Founder Archives."

The room fell silent. The Founder Archives were sealed in a climate-controlled vault, their physical books and documents so fragile that they had not been examined in living memory. All our knowledge came from digital copies, themselves copies of copies, degraded over centuries.

Stewart had been seeking an excuse to access the Archives for years. But what choice did we have?

"Permission granted," I said, and adjourned the Council.

Three weeks passed before Stewart requested another meeting. I convened the War Council at dawn, and by early afternoon we had completed the formalities and granted Stewart the floor.

"Some of you are what we term 'female,'" he began. "You know you differ from the rest of us physiologically. You have certain advantages—different hormonal profiles, different skeletal structures, different metabolic processes. And you may ask, why should this be? There is no obvious military or survival advantage to these differences. Yet they exist. Have you never wondered why?"

"General Stewart," I interrupted, "fascinating as this is, perhaps you could—"

"Of course," he said. "In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The Archives date from that era—not one document mentions our current reproductive technology. In that time, reproduction was carried on by individuals, without mechanical assistance. The females are not a separate subspecies or the result of environmental adaptation. We are all one species, with two distinct biological forms. And these forms were complementary in the reproductive process."

The room erupted in chaos. Stewart had to shout his final words: "The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional! The system still exists within us!"

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors in shock and disbelief. I realized I needed to find a flaw in Stewart's logic before the situation spiraled further out of control.

"There is a contradiction in your theory," I announced loudly. "If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines? Why abandon a working system?"

Stewart looked troubled by this question. Then Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention by the door, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig. Privately, however, I had to admit his hypothesis had merit. I authorized Stewart to continue his research.

I worried about young Nelson in the brig. He would remain there until the Council chose to release him, which required another meeting. When Stewart reported he had made a breakthrough, I immediately convened the Council, hoping to argue for the boy's release.

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book, but his appearance shocked me more than the artifact. He looked as though he hadn't slept or eaten in days. His eyes were sunken, his face gaunt. But it was the expression in those eyes that truly disturbed me—a mixture of horror and fascination.

After the formalities, Stewart spoke. "I have discovered the mechanism of biological reproduction," he said, holding up the book. "This is a pre-Founder medical manual. It's titled 'Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide.' It appears to be some sort of instructional text." He dropped the book on the table and rubbed his face.

Something in his demeanor commanded absolute attention. He continued in a low voice: "The process is... complex. And intimate. Let me start at the beginning. You see, there are certain biological structures, certain chemical processes, certain physical interactions..."

When he finished, the Council sat in horrified silence. No one cried heresy or treason. There was only stunned disbelief and the beginning of nausea.

I forced myself to speak. "Surely these biological structures you mention have atrophied? With three centuries of disuse, will they not have evolved away?"

"I don't think so," Stewart replied. "Evolutionary time scales are far longer than three centuries. And the persistence of female physiological characteristics suggests the reproductive systems remain functional, at least in some individuals."

We sat in grim silence, facing a terrible reality.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Are there any objections?"

There were none. Who would deny anything to someone willing to undergo such an ordeal for humanity's survival?

"And the male volunteer?" I asked.

"Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate," Stewart said. "They both understand what's required."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms.

Stewart gestured toward the medical bay, but Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch," he said, "would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment outdoors? The Memorial Gardens—with its soft grass and sheltering trees—would be more peaceful than the clinical environment. Perhaps the memory of the Founders will guide us."

His eyes met mine, and I understood. He was thinking of Diana's comfort and dignity. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal.

"The gardens lack proper observation facilities," I noted. "We must document this for scientific purposes."

Diana spoke up. "Sir, we understand the need for documentation. But the medical bay feels... incompatible with what we're being asked to do."

I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to the Memorial Gardens on our western ridge. The elevated grounds offered privacy and the tranquility Ryan had requested. As we walked up the winding path, I glanced back at the valley below—the agricultural domes were completely dark now, deep in the shadow our ridge cast across them each evening.

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back toward the base, both of us exhausted. It had been a horrific day. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy, the sounds...

We paused at the edge of the ridge, looking up at the stars. Behind us lay the gardens where the experiment had taken place.

"They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The manual mentions a significant time delay. The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

"It doesn't matter," I said bleakly. "We cannot ask them to repeat such an ordeal."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders protectively.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed.

I waited. Stewart remained silent.

"Sir, we wanted to tell you..." He raised his eyes to mine. "We're willing to try again."

I felt tears forming. Such sacrifice, such dedication to duty—

"We have one request," Ryan continued. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Of course," I replied. They could have anything they wanted. My relief must have been obvious, because Ryan took a deep breath and continued.

"We don't deserve special praise, sir," he said. "The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

I watched them walk away together under the stars, heading back toward the gardens.

My heart swelled with pride. I no longer feared for humanity's future when our young warriors could demonstrate such nobility and dedication to the mission.

In the morning, I would recommend them both for commendations. Perhaps even the Founder's Medal for extraordinary service to humanity.

But tonight, I simply watched them disappear into the darkness, two young soldiers willing to sacrifice their dignity and comfort for the future of our species.

Stewart cleared his throat. "I should return to my quarters. There's more research to be done."

I nodded, then turned to look back down toward the valley. Somewhere in the darkness below lay the agricultural domes—invisible now beneath our ridge's shadow, but I knew exactly where they stood. Tomorrow morning I would watch the sun rise over Northfield's territory to the east, watch its light creep across the valley floor. The domes would emerge from night gradually, their curved surfaces catching the dawn light one by one. Then would come the long productive hours before evening, when the sun would sink behind our ridge once more and plunge the domes back into early darkness.

The machines had failed us. But humanity, it seemed, would endure.
